cards.t: Node 0 · The page that cannot change
cards.q: Before any scripting existed, what was the only way to change what a user saw on a web page?
cards.a: Ask the server for an entirely new document. The browser discarded the current page and drew the replacement. The round trip was the unit of interaction.

cards.t: Node 0 · The page that cannot change
cards.q: Why did the round-trip model feel unbearable in 1994 specifically, rather than merely inelegant?
cards.a: Modems ran at 14.4 or 28.8 kilobits per second. Discovering a mistyped email address took several seconds and usually arrived on a fresh page with the rest of your input cleared.

cards.t: Node 0 · The page that cannot change
cards.q: The browser had already parsed the page and worked out where every piece of text went. Why did that not help?
cards.a: That structure existed only inside the browser and was not exposed to anything. There was no program to address it and no API through which to address it.

cards.t: Node 0 · The page that cannot change
cards.q: When did JavaScript first ship in a browser, and in which product?
cards.a: Netscape Navigator 2.0, in March 1996.

cards.t: Node 0 · The page that cannot change
cards.q: What is retroactively called “DOM Level 0”?
cards.a: The handful of collections Netscape exposed with the first JavaScript — document.forms, document.images, document.links and similar. It was accreted rather than designed.

cards.t: Node 0 · The page that cannot change
cards.q: What could DOM Level 0 realistically accomplish?
cards.a: Checking whether a form field was empty before submitting. It was enough for validation and nowhere near enough to build an interface.

cards.t: Node 0 · The page that cannot change
cards.q: How did Internet Explorer 4 and Netscape Navigator 4 expose the page, and why was that a disaster?
cards.a: IE4 used document.all, Navigator 4 used document.layers. They were incompatible, so any page doing real work contained two implementations of itself.

cards.t: Node 0 · The page that cannot change
cards.q: What specific problem did the W3C DOM standardisation effort exist to solve?
cards.a: The absence of a single, complete, agreed model of the page that a program could address the same way in every browser.

cards.t: Node 0 · The page that cannot change
cards.q: State the limitation at the end of Node 0 in one sentence.
cards.a: You can reach a few named collections someone thought to expose, in two mutually incompatible dialects, and nothing else.

cards.t: Node 1 · The page as a tree of live objects
cards.q: When was DOM Level 1 published, and by whom?
cards.a: The W3C, as a Recommendation, in October 1998.

cards.t: Node 1 · The page as a tree of live objects
cards.q: State DOM Level 1's central idea.
cards.a: When the browser parses HTML it builds an object graph in memory mirroring the markup's structure, and exposes that graph to JavaScript. That graph is the Document Object Model.

cards.t: Node 1 · The page as a tree of live objects
cards.q: Give the one-sentence definition of the DOM that resolves most later confusion.
cards.a: The DOM is not the HTML and not the pixels — it is a live object graph sitting between them.

cards.t: Node 1 · The page as a tree of live objects
cards.q: What happens to the HTML string once the page has loaded?
cards.a: It is parsed exactly once and is then irrelevant to the running page. Only the tree of objects remains.

cards.t: Node 1 · The page as a tree of live objects
cards.q: Are DOM nodes real JavaScript objects?
cards.a: Yes. Every node is a genuine JavaScript-reachable object with properties and methods, backed by the browser's internal representation.

cards.t: Node 1 · The page as a tree of live objects
cards.q: Name the main kinds of node in the tree.
cards.a: Element nodes (a tag), text nodes (a run of characters), comment nodes, and the document node at the top.

cards.t: Node 1 · The page as a tree of live objects
cards.q: Is the document node an element?
cards.a: No. It has no tag and is not an element. It sits above the root element and is reached through the global document.

cards.t: Node 1 · The page as a tree of live objects
cards.q: What is document.documentElement?
cards.a: The single root element node of the tree — the <html> element. document.head and document.body sit beneath it.

cards.t: Node 1 · The page as a tree of live objects
cards.q: What does each node know about its neighbours?
cards.a: Its parent, its children in document order, and its siblings. The tree is navigable in every direction from any node.

cards.t: Node 1 · The page as a tree of live objects
cards.q: Why might the tree the browser built differ from the markup you wrote?
cards.a: The HTML parser is specified to repair broken markup — closing unclosed tags, relocating a stray element out of a table, dropping a <p> nested inside a <p>. You get the repaired result.

cards.t: Node 1 · The page as a tree of live objects
cards.q: What happens to the whitespace between tags in your source?
cards.a: It becomes real text nodes. A <ul> with each <li> on its own line has text nodes containing newlines and spaces between the items.

cards.t: Node 1 · The page as a tree of live objects
cards.q: Why does the whitespace-text-node fact matter beyond trivia?
cards.a: It makes firstChild, childNodes and nextSibling return whitespace rather than the element you expected, which is a permanent source of bugs.

cards.t: Node 1 · The page as a tree of live objects
cards.q: What is the difference between viewing source and the Elements panel in DevTools?
cards.a: View source shows the original HTML string as sent. The Elements panel shows the current DOM tree — after parser repair and after every change your scripts have made.

cards.t: Node 1 · The page as a tree of live objects
cards.q: State what is still broken at the end of Node 1.
cards.a: You have a tree and a handle on its root, but reaching a specific node deep inside means walking down child by child, which is unusable.

cards.q: What does document.getElementById(id) return when nothing matches?
cards.a: null. Not undefined, not an empty collection — null.

cards.q: Why is getElementById the fastest lookup in the DOM?
cards.a: Browsers maintain an internal map from id to element, so it is a hash lookup rather than a tree search.

cards.q: What do getElementsByTagName and getElementsByClassName return?
cards.a: A live HTMLCollection — not an array and not a snapshot.

cards.q: What does it mean for an HTMLCollection to be live?
cards.a: It is a standing query, not a snapshot. Append a matching element to the document and the collection you are already holding grows, with no action from you.

cards.q: Describe the classic infinite loop caused by a live collection.
cards.a: Iterating the collection by index while appending a matching element inside the loop. The collection grows exactly as fast as the index advances, so the loop never terminates.

cards.q: When did browsers begin shipping the Selectors API, and when was it a W3C Recommendation?
cards.a: Shipped in Safari 3.1 (2008) and Internet Explorer 8 (2009); W3C Recommendation in February 2013.

cards.q: What do querySelector and querySelectorAll return?
cards.a: querySelector returns the first matching element or null. querySelectorAll returns a static NodeList of all matches.

cards.q: What is the real significance of the Selectors API, beyond convenience?
cards.a: The same language that describes which elements a style applies to now describes which elements a script operates on. No new vocabulary is required of anyone who has written CSS.

cards.q: What did the Selectors API do to jQuery's value proposition?
cards.a: It made jQuery's core selling point — cross-browser CSS-selector querying — redundant, roughly a decade after jQuery 1.0 shipped in August 2006.

cards.q: Is the NodeList from querySelectorAll live or static?
cards.a: Static. It is a snapshot at the moment of the call and does not change when the document does.

cards.q: Is a NodeList an array?
cards.a: No. It has forEach, length and indexing, but no map, filter or reduce. Use Array.from(list) or [...list].

cards.q: Does element.children have forEach?
cards.a: No. It is a live HTMLCollection, which has neither forEach nor the array methods. This asymmetry with NodeList is a routine source of confusion.

cards.q: Which selection methods are available on elements and not only on document?
cards.a: All of them except getElementById, which exists only on document (and on document fragments). querySelector, querySelectorAll, getElementsByTagName and getElementsByClassName all work from any element.

cards.q: Why scope a query to a subtree rather than searching from document?
cards.a: It is faster and far less fragile — a selector scoped to a container cannot accidentally match an identically-classed element elsewhere on the page.

cards.q: Does querySelectorAll use the browser's real CSS selector engine?
cards.a: Yes — the same engine used for style matching, so any selector valid in a stylesheet works, including pseudo-classes like :last-child and attribute selectors like [href^="/docs"].

cards.q: What does container.querySelector(':scope > .row') do that container.querySelector('.row') does not?
cards.a: :scope anchors the selector at the container itself, so :scope > .row matches only direct children. Without it, a descendant combinator matches at any depth.

cards.q: State the limitation at the end of Node 2.
cards.a: Selectors describe patterns of elements. They cannot express relative position, cannot reach text or comment nodes, and cannot answer questions about a node's neighbours.

cards.q: Name the DOM Level 1 traversal properties that walk all nodes.
cards.a: parentNode, childNodes, firstChild, lastChild, nextSibling, previousSibling.

cards.q: Name the element-only traversal properties.
cards.a: parentElement, children, firstElementChild, lastElementChild, nextElementSibling, previousElementSibling.

cards.q: Why do both vocabularies exist?
cards.a: The DOM must describe documents in general, where text nodes are the actual content rather than an artefact of formatting. Application code almost always wants the element-only set.

cards.q: When do parentNode and parentElement differ?
cards.a: Only for the root <html> element. Its parentNode is the document node; its parentElement is null, because the document is not an element.

cards.q: What are nodeType values 1, 3, 8 and 9?
cards.a: 1 element, 3 text, 8 comment, 9 document. The numbers are arbitrary — just the enumeration order in the 1998 spec.

cards.q: How does modern code usually test node kind instead of nodeType?
cards.a: instanceof Element, instanceof Text, or checking tagName. nodeType integers survive in older code and library internals.

cards.q: What does element.closest(selector) do?
cards.a: Walks upward from the element through its ancestors, including the element itself, and returns the first match, or null.

cards.q: When did closest() ship?
cards.a: Chrome 41, in 2015.

cards.q: What is element.matches(selector)?
cards.a: A boolean test: does this element itself match this CSS selector? Useful in delegated handlers and filters.

cards.q: What does a.contains(b) return when a === b?
cards.a: true. contains treats a node as containing itself.

cards.q: What are TreeWalker and NodeIterator for?
cards.a: Visiting every node of a chosen kind in document order, created with document.createTreeWalker(root, whatToShow, filter). They exist mainly for text processing — find-and-highlight, text extraction, spellchecking.

cards.q: How common is TreeWalker in application code?
cards.a: Rare. Most application developers never write one. It is genuinely useful in editors and tooling.

cards.q: Why is closest() structurally important rather than merely handy?
cards.a: It is what makes event delegation robust — given the deepest element a click landed on, it finds the meaningful ancestor you actually care about.

cards.q: State the limitation at the end of Node 3.
cards.a: You can reach any node from any other node, and you still cannot change a single character of what any of them says.

cards.t: Node 4 · Changing what a node says
cards.q: What does setting textContent do to the element's existing children?
cards.a: Discards all of them and replaces them with a single text node.

cards.t: Node 4 · Changing what a node says
cards.q: If you assign a string containing <script> to textContent, what appears on screen?
cards.a: The literal characters <script>. Nothing is parsed and nothing executes.

cards.t: Node 4 · Changing what a node says
cards.q: What is the correct default for displaying a value from a user, a database, or an API?
cards.a: textContent. It treats everything as literal characters, which removes the injection question entirely.

cards.t: Node 4 · Changing what a node says
cards.q: What does assigning to innerHTML actually invoke?
cards.a: The HTML parser. Your string is parsed, a subtree is built from the result, and the element's existing children are replaced by it.

cards.t: Node 4 · Changing what a node says
cards.q: Where did innerHTML come from?
cards.a: Microsoft invented it for Internet Explorer 4, in 1997. It was so convenient that everyone copied it, and it was standardised long afterwards.

cards.t: Node 4 · Changing what a node says
cards.q: Does a <script> tag inserted via innerHTML execute?
cards.a: No — the HTML spec explicitly disables it. This provides almost no protection, because <img src=x onerror="..."> and dozens of equivalents work perfectly.

cards.t: Node 4 · Changing what a node says
cards.q: What is the difference between textContent and innerText?
cards.a: textContent returns what is in the tree, including text inside display: none, with source whitespace intact. innerText returns what is rendered — roughly what you would get by selecting with a mouse and copying.

cards.t: Node 4 · Changing what a node says
cards.q: Why can reading innerText be expensive when reading textContent never is?
cards.a: To report what is rendered, the browser may have to compute layout. textContent is answerable from the tree alone.

cards.t: Node 4 · Changing what a node says
cards.q: Does innerText respect display: none?
cards.a: Yes — hidden text is excluded. textContent includes it.

cards.t: Node 4 · Changing what a node says
cards.q: What does outerHTML include that innerHTML does not?
cards.a: The element's own opening and closing tags, not just its contents. Assigning to it replaces the element itself.

cards.t: Node 4 · Changing what a node says
cards.q: What do nodeValue and data do on a text node?
cards.a: Both get or set the characters the text node holds. Text nodes also support appendData, insertData and splitText.

cards.t: Node 4 · Changing what a node says
cards.q: How common is direct text-node surgery?
cards.a: Rare in application code, central in rich-text editors, which need to split and merge text nodes constantly.

cards.t: Node 4 · Changing what a node says
cards.q: State the limitation at the end of Node 4.
cards.a: Content is only part of what an element is. A checkbox's checkedness, a link's destination, a button's disabledness, and an element's classes and styling are not content and none are reachable yet.

cards.q: State the attribute-versus-property distinction in one sentence.
cards.a: Attributes are what was written in the HTML; properties are fields on the JavaScript object. Two storage locations, loosely synchronised by non-uniform rules.

cards.q: What type are attribute values, always?
cards.a: Strings. There are no other types on the attribute side.

cards.q: What does el.setAttribute('disabled', false) do?
cards.a: Disables the element. The attribute is set to the string "false", and HTML boolean attributes are true when present regardless of value. Use el.disabled = false or removeAttribute.

cards.q: What type is el.disabled on the property side?
cards.a: A genuine boolean. Likewise el.hidden is a boolean and el.tabIndex is a number — properties have real types, attributes do not.

cards.q: What does “reflection” mean between attributes and properties?
cards.a: Change one side and the other follows. Most attributes reflect; some reflect with transformation; a few deliberately do not stay in sync at all.

cards.q: Why does el.href not equal the string you wrote in the markup?
cards.a: The href attribute reflects into the property as the fully resolved absolute URL. href="/docs" reads back as https://example.com/docs. Use getAttribute('href') for the literal.

cards.q: What is the relationship between input.value and the value attribute?
cards.a: The attribute is the initial value only. Once a user types, input.value reflects what they typed and getAttribute('value') still returns the original.

cards.q: Why do defaultValue and defaultChecked exist?
cards.a: To give a property-side name for the attribute-side value, since value and checked properties track live state instead.

cards.q: Which React concept does the value/attribute split directly explain?
cards.a: Controlled versus uncontrolled inputs. React's value prop drives the live property; defaultValue sets the attribute and lets the DOM own the state.

cards.q: What is the sanctioned way to attach your own data to an element?
cards.a: data-* attributes, read through the dataset property. data-user-id="42" becomes el.dataset.userId.

cards.q: What type is everything in dataset?
cards.a: String. data-count="3" gives "3", not 3.

cards.q: How does dataset convert names?
cards.a: Kebab-case to camelCase: data-user-id becomes dataset.userId.

cards.q: What does classList give you over className?
cards.a: add, remove, toggle, contains and replace, each accepting multiple arguments — instead of error-prone string manipulation.

cards.q: What does the second argument to classList.toggle do?
cards.a: It sets rather than flips. classList.toggle('open', isOpen) adds when isOpen is true and removes when false.

cards.q: When did classList become widely available?
cards.a: Around 2010–2011 — Firefox 3.6 and Chrome 8 era — standardised with HTML5 and DOM4.

cards.q: What exactly does element.style.color read?
cards.a: The inline style only, i.e. the element's style attribute. If the colour came from a stylesheet, this is the empty string.

cards.q: What does getComputedStyle(element) return?
cards.a: The fully resolved value in effect after every stylesheet, cascade rule and inheritance has been applied. It may require layout to be up to date, so it is not free.

cards.q: How are CSS property names spelled on element.style?
cards.a: camelCased — backgroundColor, borderTopWidth.

cards.q: How do you set a CSS custom property from JavaScript?
cards.a: el.style.setProperty('--accent', 'tomato'), and read it with getComputedStyle(el).getPropertyValue('--accent'). Custom properties keep their literal names and are not camelCased.

cards.q: State the limitation at the end of Node 5.
cards.a: Everything so far modifies elements that already exist. An interface that grows — a list gaining rows, a dialog appearing, a table rendered from fetched data — needs nodes that were never in the original HTML.

cards.q: What does document.createElement('div') return, and where is it?
cards.a: A real element node that is not in the document. It has no parent, occupies no space, and is invisible.

cards.q: Why is construction separated from insertion?
cards.a: So you can build a subtree completely before the user ever sees a partial version of it, and so a single insertion carries the whole thing.

cards.q: Name the DOM Level 1 insertion and removal methods.
cards.a: appendChild, insertBefore, removeChild, replaceChild — all called on the parent.

cards.q: What is awkward about insertBefore?
cards.a: It requires a reference to the node you want to precede, so inserting after something means computing nextSibling first — and passing null as the reference appends.

cards.q: Name the modern insertion methods and when they shipped.
cards.a: append, prepend, before, after, replaceWith, remove — Chrome 54 (October 2016) and Firefox 49 (September 2016).

cards.q: Give two advantages of append over appendChild.
cards.a: It accepts multiple arguments, and it accepts plain strings, which become text nodes safely — no parsing, no injection risk.

cards.q: What does el.remove() improve on?
cards.a: It needs no reference to the parent, unlike parent.removeChild(el).

cards.q: What happens if you insert a node that is already in the document?
cards.a: It moves. A node has exactly one parent, so there is no insertion operation that duplicates.

cards.q: How do you actually duplicate a node?
cards.a: node.cloneNode(deep), where deep controls whether descendants come along.

cards.q: Does cloneNode copy event listeners?
cards.a: No. Listeners are not part of the node's data, so the clone has none.

cards.q: What is a DocumentFragment and what is it for?
cards.a: A lightweight, parentless container from document.createDocumentFragment(). Append many nodes into it, then append the fragment once — it dissolves, delivering its children in a single document mutation.

cards.q: What is the <template> element?
cards.a: An HTML element whose contents are parsed but inert — not rendered, not executed, images not fetched. You clone template.content into place when needed.

cards.q: What does insertAdjacentHTML do, and what are its four positions?
cards.a: Parses a markup string and inserts it without rebuilding the element's existing children. Positions: 'beforebegin', 'afterbegin', 'beforeend', 'afterend'.

cards.q: Why is el.innerHTML += '...' a trap?
cards.a: It serialises the entire existing subtree to a string, concatenates, and reparses the whole thing — destroying every existing node, and with them every event listener, form state and node reference.

cards.q: What is insertAdjacentElement and insertAdjacentText?
cards.a: The same four-position insertion for an existing element node and for literal text respectively, without invoking the HTML parser.

cards.q: What is document.importNode(node, deep) for?
cards.a: Copying a node from another document (from DOMParser, an iframe, or a template's document) so it can be inserted into this one.

cards.q: State the limitation at the end of Node 6.
cards.a: All of this is one-directional. Your script decides when things happen; the page still cannot respond to a click, a keystroke, a scroll, or a form submission.

cards.q: What is a DOM event, precisely?
cards.a: An object the browser creates when something notable happens, and delivers to code that registered interest in it.

cards.q: What is the fatal structural limit of el.onclick = fn?
cards.a: There is one slot. Assigning a second time silently replaces the first handler, so two independent pieces of code cannot both listen.

cards.q: What is the additional problem with inline onclick="..." attributes?
cards.a: The attribute value is a string evaluated as code in the global scope — exactly what a Content Security Policy exists to forbid.

cards.q: When was addEventListener standardised?
cards.a: DOM Level 2 Events, a W3C Recommendation in November 2000.

cards.q: What does addEventListener fix?
cards.a: Any number of listeners can coexist on one element for one event type, and each is removable independently.

cards.q: What must removeEventListener be given?
cards.a: The same function reference that was added, plus a matching capture setting. Two identical-looking arrow functions are two different objects and will not match.

cards.q: Why does passing an inline arrow to both add and remove silently fail?
cards.a: Each arrow expression creates a new function object. removeEventListener compares by identity, finds no match, and removes nothing — with no error.

cards.q: Name the options in addEventListener's third argument.
cards.a: capture, once, passive, and signal. Historically the third argument was a bare boolean meaning capture.

cards.q: What does once: true do?
cards.a: Removes the listener automatically after it fires once.

cards.q: What does passive: true promise, and why does the browser care?
cards.a: It promises the handler will not call preventDefault. Without that promise the browser must wait for your touchstart or wheel handler to finish before it knows whether it may scroll, so a slow handler stalls scrolling itself.

cards.q: What did Chrome 56 change in January 2017?
cards.a: It made touchstart and touchmove listeners on document passive by default, changing behaviour on the live web to protect scroll performance.

cards.q: What does the signal option accept, and when did it ship?
cards.a: An AbortSignal from an AbortController. Added to addEventListener in Chrome 90, April 2021.

cards.q: What properties does every event carry?
cards.a: type, target, currentTarget, timeStamp, bubbles, cancelable, defaultPrevented, and eventPhase.

cards.q: What does a MouseEvent carry beyond the base event?
cards.a: clientX/clientY (viewport coordinates), pageX/pageY (document coordinates), button, and the modifier flags shiftKey, ctrlKey, altKey, metaKey.

cards.q: How do you create and fire your own event?
cards.a: const e = new CustomEvent('cart:updated', { detail: {...}, bubbles: true }) then el.dispatchEvent(e).

cards.q: Why is a custom event useful architecturally?
cards.a: It lets one part of a page tell another that something happened without either holding a reference to the other.

cards.q: Where does the payload of a CustomEvent live?
cards.a: In event.detail, set via the detail option at construction.

cards.q: State the limitation at the end of Node 7.
cards.a: A listener is attached to one specific element. Five hundred rows means five hundred listeners, and rows created after the listeners were attached have none.

cards.q: Name the three phases of event propagation, in order.
cards.a: Capture (root downward), target (the deepest element), bubble (back up to the root).

cards.q: Which phase does addEventListener register for by default?
cards.a: The bubble phase. Passing capture: true registers for the downward pass instead.

cards.q: Why do both capture and bubble exist at all?
cards.a: Netscape and Microsoft implemented opposite models during the browser wars. DOM Level 2 resolved the argument by specifying both and letting the developer choose.

cards.q: Define event delegation.
cards.a: Attaching one listener to a common ancestor instead of one per child, then inspecting the event to decide which descendant it concerns.

cards.q: Give the two reasons delegation matters.
cards.a: It replaces N listeners with one, and it covers elements that do not exist yet, because the listener was never attached to them in the first place.

cards.q: Why is matching on e.target alone fragile in a delegated handler?
cards.a: e.target is the deepest element hit, which may be an icon or text span inside the button rather than the button. e.target.closest('button.delete') walks up to the element you meant.

cards.q: Distinguish e.target from e.currentTarget.
cards.a: e.target is where the event originated and never changes as it travels. e.currentTarget is the element whose listener is running right now, and changes at each step.

cards.q: What is this inside a non-arrow event handler?
cards.a: e.currentTarget — the element the listener was attached to.

cards.q: What does stopPropagation() do?
cards.a: Stops the event travelling further along the path, so ancestors (or descendants, in capture) never receive it.

cards.q: How does stopImmediatePropagation() differ?
cards.a: It additionally prevents any other listeners on the same element from running.

cards.q: Does stopPropagation prevent the browser's default behaviour?
cards.a: No. That is preventDefault. The two are entirely independent.

cards.q: Why is calling stopPropagation reflexively a real bug?
cards.a: It breaks every delegated listener above it — analytics, dropdown-close handlers, framework internals — for reasons invisible at the call site.

cards.q: Name events that do not bubble.
cards.a: focus, blur, load, error, scroll on an element, and mouseenter/mouseleave.

cards.q: What are focusin and focusout for?
cards.a: They are the bubbling equivalents of focus and blur, and exist specifically so focus can be delegated.

cards.q: How do you check at runtime whether an event bubbles?
cards.a: e.bubbles.

cards.q: What is the difference between mouseover and mouseenter?
cards.a: mouseover bubbles and fires again when the pointer moves onto a child. mouseenter does not bubble and fires only when entering the element's boundary — usually what you want for hover UI.

cards.q: Write the canonical delegated click handler.
cards.a: table.addEventListener('click', e => { const b = e.target.closest('button.delete'); if (!b || !table.contains(b)) return; removeRow(b.closest('tr')); })

cards.q: Why include the table.contains(btn) check?
cards.a: closest can walk past the delegating container if the event came from a nested detached or shadow context; the check confirms the match is genuinely inside the region you are handling.

cards.q: State the limitation at the end of Node 8.
cards.a: Stopping an event from travelling does nothing about what the browser itself does. A form still submits and reloads, a link still navigates, and everything your script did is discarded.

cards.t: Node 9 · Default actions, forms and input
cards.q: What is a default action?
cards.a: The browser's own built-in reaction to certain events, which runs after listeners unless cancelled — navigating on a link click, submitting on a form submit, moving focus on Tab.

cards.t: Node 9 · Default actions, forms and input
cards.q: What exactly does preventDefault() cancel?
cards.a: The native behaviour, and only that. It does not affect propagation.

cards.t: Node 9 · Default actions, forms and input
cards.q: Which events cannot be cancelled, and how do you know?
cards.a: Those with e.cancelable === false. scroll is the notable one — it must be prevented at its source on wheel or touchmove, or with CSS.

cards.t: Node 9 · Default actions, forms and input
cards.q: How do you check whether some earlier listener already cancelled an event?
cards.a: e.defaultPrevented.

cards.t: Node 9 · Default actions, forms and input
cards.q: Which single line of code is the origin of the single-page application?
cards.a: e.preventDefault() in a submit handler — cancel the navigation, read the values, send them with fetch, update the DOM. The page never reloads.

cards.t: Node 9 · Default actions, forms and input
cards.q: What does new FormData(formElement) collect?
cards.a: Every named control's current value, handling file inputs and multi-selects correctly. It can be passed straight to fetch as a body.

cards.t: Node 9 · Default actions, forms and input
cards.q: Why must form controls have a name attribute?
cards.a: FormData and native submission both key on name. A control without one is simply not included.

cards.t: Node 9 · Default actions, forms and input
cards.q: What is input.validity?
cards.a: A ValidityState object with boolean flags: valueMissing, typeMismatch, patternMismatch, tooShort, tooLong, rangeOverflow, rangeUnderflow, stepMismatch, customError, and valid.

cards.t: Node 9 · Default actions, forms and input
cards.q: Distinguish checkValidity() from reportValidity().
cards.a: checkValidity() tests silently and returns a boolean. reportValidity() tests and displays the browser's own validation message.

cards.t: Node 9 · Default actions, forms and input
cards.q: What does setCustomValidity(message) achieve?
cards.a: It makes your own rule participate in native validation rather than sitting beside it. A non-empty message marks the field invalid; an empty string clears it.

cards.t: Node 9 · Default actions, forms and input
cards.q: Distinguish the input event from the change event.
cards.a: input fires on every change to the value as it happens. change fires when the value is committed — on blur for text fields, immediately for checkboxes, radios and selects.

cards.t: Node 9 · Default actions, forms and input
cards.q: Why are keydown/keyup unreliable for tracking a field's value?
cards.a: A key press may produce no character, an IME may produce one character from several presses, and a paste or drag produces text with no key press at all.

cards.t: Node 9 · Default actions, forms and input
cards.q: State the rule for choosing between input and keydown.
cards.a: If you care about the value, listen to input. If you care about the key, listen to keydown.

cards.t: Node 9 · Default actions, forms and input
cards.q: What is the status of keypress?
cards.a: Deprecated. It should not appear in new code.

cards.t: Node 9 · Default actions, forms and input
cards.q: Distinguish e.key from e.code.
cards.a: e.key is the character or named key produced — "a", "Enter", "ArrowLeft". e.code is the physical key position regardless of layout — "KeyA".

cards.t: Node 9 · Default actions, forms and input
cards.q: Which of key and code do keyboard shortcuts usually want?
cards.a: key, because it reflects what the user actually typed on their layout. code suits games and layout-independent bindings.

cards.t: Node 9 · Default actions, forms and input
cards.q: What is the status of e.keyCode?
cards.a: Deprecated and inconsistent across browsers and layouts. Use key or code.

cards.t: Node 9 · Default actions, forms and input
cards.q: Name the clipboard events and where their data lives.
cards.a: copy, cut, paste — data is on e.clipboardData.

cards.t: Node 9 · Default actions, forms and input
cards.q: What is the notorious gotcha in HTML drag and drop?
cards.a: dragover must have its default prevented, or drop never fires at all.

cards.t: Node 9 · Default actions, forms and input
cards.q: What do pointer events unify?
cards.a: Mouse, touch and stylus into one model — pointerdown, pointermove, pointerup, with e.pointerType telling you which. New code should prefer them over separate mouse and touch handling.

cards.t: Node 9 · Default actions, forms and input
cards.q: What does setPointerCapture solve?
cards.a: It routes all subsequent pointer events for that pointer to one element, so a drag continues correctly even when the pointer leaves the element's bounds.

cards.t: Node 9 · Default actions, forms and input
cards.q: State the limitation at the end of Node 9.
cards.a: Form controls are a fixed vocabulary. Anything richer, where a user selects a span of text across elements and formats it, is outside all of this.

cards.t: Node 10 · Selection, ranges and editable content
cards.q: What is a Range?
cards.a: A pair of boundary points in the tree — a start node with an offset and an end node with an offset — describing a contiguous stretch of content that may cross element boundaries.

cards.t: Node 10 · Selection, ranges and editable content
cards.q: Can a Range's endpoints sit inside different elements?
cards.a: Yes. That is the whole point — a range can start halfway through a text node inside a <strong> and end inside a different paragraph.

cards.t: Node 10 · Selection, ranges and editable content
cards.q: How do you create a Range programmatically?
cards.a: document.createRange(), then setStart(node, offset) and setEnd(node, offset).

cards.t: Node 10 · Selection, ranges and editable content
cards.q: Name operations a Range supports.
cards.a: extractContents, cloneContents, deleteContents, surroundContents, insertNode, and getBoundingClientRect.

cards.t: Node 10 · Selection, ranges and editable content
cards.q: What does window.getSelection() return?
cards.a: A Selection object describing what the user has highlighted, expressed as one or more ranges.

cards.t: Node 10 · Selection, ranges and editable content
cards.q: How do you get the highlighted text and the underlying range?
cards.a: selection.toString() for the text; selection.getRangeAt(0) for the range.

cards.t: Node 10 · Selection, ranges and editable content
cards.q: How do you set the selection programmatically?
cards.a: selection.removeAllRanges() followed by selection.addRange(range).

cards.t: Node 10 · Selection, ranges and editable content
cards.q: Which event fires as the selection changes?
cards.a: selectionchange, on the document.

cards.t: Node 10 · Selection, ranges and editable content
cards.q: What does the contenteditable attribute do?
cards.a: Turns any element into an editable region, giving you caret handling, selection, and native editing behaviour for free.

cards.t: Node 10 · Selection, ranges and editable content
cards.q: Why do serious editors like ProseMirror, Slate and Lexical not rely on contenteditable's own behaviour?
cards.a: Browsers historically produced different markup for the same operation. Those editors maintain their own document model and treat contenteditable purely as an input surface, reconciling what the browser did back into the model on every change.

cards.t: Node 10 · Selection, ranges and editable content
cards.q: What is the status of document.execCommand?
cards.a: Long deprecated. It was the original formatting API for contenteditable and produced inconsistent markup across browsers.

cards.t: Node 10 · Selection, ranges and editable content
cards.q: What is the honest depth target for this node?
cards.a: Know that ranges and selection exist, know why rich-text editing is hard, and reach for an existing editor. Do not build one from scratch.

cards.t: Node 10 · Selection, ranges and editable content
cards.q: State the limitation at the end of Node 10.
cards.a: An editor needs a formatting toolbar positioned next to the selection, and nothing so far can answer where anything is on screen.

cards.q: What does getBoundingClientRect() return?
cards.a: The element's rectangle — top, right, bottom, left, width, height, x, y — in viewport coordinates, accounting for CSS transforms.

cards.q: Why does getBoundingClientRect() change as the user scrolls?
cards.a: Because it is relative to the visible window, not the document.

cards.q: How do you convert a client rect to document coordinates?
cards.a: Add window.scrollX to the horizontal values and window.scrollY to the vertical ones.

cards.q: What does offsetWidth include?
cards.a: Content, padding, border, and the scrollbar if present. It is an integer.

cards.q: What does clientWidth include?
cards.a: Content and padding. It excludes border and scrollbar.

cards.q: What does scrollHeight measure?
cards.a: The full height of the content including the part scrolled out of view, plus padding.

cards.q: What is offsetTop relative to?
cards.a: offsetParent — the nearest positioned ancestor. This makes it layout-dependent and awkward, which is why getBoundingClientRect is generally preferred.

cards.q: Is scrollTop writable?
cards.a: Yes. Assigning to it scrolls the element, which is the low-level way to scroll something programmatically.

cards.q: Give the expression for “how far from the bottom is this scrolling element”.
cards.a: el.scrollHeight - el.scrollTop - el.clientHeight. When it approaches zero the user has scrolled to the bottom — the basis of infinite scroll.

cards.q: Name the viewport-scrolling methods.
cards.a: window.scrollTo({ top, behavior: 'smooth' }) and window.scrollBy.

cards.q: Why prefer element.scrollIntoView() over manual arithmetic?
cards.a: It does the arithmetic for you and correctly handles nested scroll containers. Its options are behavior, block and inline.

cards.q: What is window.devicePixelRatio?
cards.a: How many physical screen pixels one CSS pixel occupies — 1 on an older monitor, 2 or 3 on a modern phone or Retina display. It exists because a CSS pixel is a unit of apparent size, not of hardware.

cards.q: What does visualViewport describe that the window dimensions do not?
cards.a: The actually visible region on mobile when the on-screen keyboard is up or the user has pinch-zoomed.

cards.q: Distinguish clientX from pageX on a mouse event.
cards.a: clientX is relative to the viewport; pageX is relative to the document and therefore includes scroll offset.

cards.q: State the limitation at the end of Node 11.
cards.a: Every one of these reads is expensive in a way nothing so far has explained, and mixing them with writes can make a correct interface unusably slow.

cards.t: Node 12 · What a mutation actually costs
cards.q: Name the four stages of the browser's rendering pipeline.
cards.a: Style (which rules apply), layout/reflow (position and size of every box), paint (filling pixels per layer), composite (assembling layers into a frame).

cards.t: Node 12 · What a mutation actually costs
cards.q: Does the browser run the pipeline on every DOM write?
cards.a: No. It batches. A hundred appends and fifty style changes in one function are queued and processed once, before the next paint.

cards.t: Node 12 · What a mutation actually costs
cards.q: So why is “DOM writes are slow” misleading advice?
cards.a: The writes are cheap and already batched. What costs is forcing the pipeline to run, which is a different and avoidable mistake.

cards.t: Node 12 · What a mutation actually costs
cards.q: What is a forced synchronous layout?
cards.a: Reading a property whose answer requires up-to-date layout while changes are still queued, so the browser must run layout immediately to answer truthfully.

cards.t: Node 12 · What a mutation actually costs
cards.q: Name properties whose reads can force layout.
cards.a: getBoundingClientRect(), offsetTop/offsetHeight, clientWidth/clientHeight, scrollTop/scrollHeight, getComputedStyle(...), and innerText.

cards.t: Node 12 · What a mutation actually costs
cards.q: Define layout thrashing.
cards.a: Interleaving reads and writes in a loop, so each write invalidates layout and each read forces it to be recomputed. N items produce N full layouts instead of one.

cards.t: Node 12 · What a mutation actually costs
cards.q: What is the fix for layout thrashing?
cards.a: Read everything first, then write everything. Separating the phases turns N layouts into one.

cards.t: Node 12 · What a mutation actually costs
cards.q: Where does the 16.7 millisecond figure come from?
cards.a: One second divided by a 60Hz refresh rate. Everything for a frame — your JavaScript, style, layout, paint, composite — must fit inside it or a frame is dropped and the interface visibly stutters.

cards.t: Node 12 · What a mutation actually costs
cards.q: What does requestAnimationFrame(callback) do?
cards.a: Schedules a callback to run just before the next paint, aligning your visual work with the browser's own rhythm.

cards.t: Node 12 · What a mutation actually costs
cards.q: Give two advantages of requestAnimationFrame over setInterval for animation.
cards.a: It runs at the display's actual cadence rather than a guessed interval, and it stops entirely when the tab is hidden, which setInterval does not.

cards.t: Node 12 · What a mutation actually costs
cards.q: When did requestAnimationFrame become available?
cards.a: Around 2011 — Chrome 10 and Firefox 4.

cards.t: Node 12 · What a mutation actually costs
cards.q: What is requestIdleCallback for?
cards.a: Scheduling non-urgent work for whatever time is left over in a frame. Shipped in Chrome 47.

cards.t: Node 12 · What a mutation actually costs
cards.q: Why prefer animating transform and opacity?
cards.a: They can usually be handled entirely by the compositor, skipping layout and paint. Animating left or width re-runs layout on every frame.

cards.t: Node 12 · What a mutation actually costs
cards.q: What does will-change tell the browser?
cards.a: That a property is about to be animated, so it can promote the element to its own layer in advance. Overusing it wastes memory — it is a hint, not a fix.

cards.t: Node 12 · What a mutation actually costs
cards.q: State the limitation at the end of Node 12.
cards.a: You know when you change the DOM. You do not know when the browser or the user changes something you care about, and polling for it is exactly the frame-budget disaster just described.

cards.q: What is the shared shape of every DOM observer?
cards.a: new XObserver(callback), then .observe(target, options), and .disconnect() to stop.

cards.q: What is the point of an observer over a polling event handler?
cards.a: The work of detecting the condition happens inside the browser rather than in your code on every scroll or resize event, and notifications are batched and asynchronous.

cards.q: What does IntersectionObserver tell you, and when did it ship?
cards.a: When an element enters or leaves a viewport or another element, at thresholds you specify. Chrome 51, May 2016.

cards.q: Name four things IntersectionObserver replaces.
cards.a: Lazy-loading images, infinite scroll, scroll-spy navigation highlighting, and impression tracking — all of which were previously scroll handlers measuring every element.

cards.q: What does rootMargin do?
cards.a: Expands or shrinks the root's bounding box for intersection purposes, so you can fire early — loading an image 200 pixels before it becomes visible.

cards.q: What does the threshold option mean?
cards.a: The ratio or ratios of visibility at which the callback fires. 0 means any pixel, 1 means fully visible, and an array gives you several trigger points.

cards.q: What does ResizeObserver solve, and when did it ship?
cards.a: It reports when a specific element changes size for any reason — window resize, a sibling growing, content changing, a CSS change. Chrome 64, January 2018.

cards.q: What was impossible before ResizeObserver?
cards.a: Component-level responsive behaviour. There was no way to know an element had resized unless the window did.

cards.q: What causes “ResizeObserver loop limit exceeded”?
cards.a: A callback that resizes the element it observes, creating a cycle. The browser detects it and reports the error rather than hanging.

cards.q: What does MutationObserver report, and when did it ship?
cards.a: Changes to the DOM tree itself — children added or removed, attributes changed, text modified — under a subtree you specify. Chrome 18, 2012.

cards.q: What did MutationObserver replace, and why?
cards.a: Mutation Events, a DOM Level 2 feature deprecated in 2011 because they fired synchronously on every single change and could make a page an order of magnitude slower.

cards.q: When is MutationObserver the right tool in application code?
cards.a: As a last resort — usually when you must react to a third-party script's changes to the DOM. In browser extensions and tooling it is everywhere.

cards.q: What does PerformanceObserver deliver?
cards.a: Timing entries, including the Largest Contentful Paint, Cumulative Layout Shift and Interaction to Next Paint measurements that make up Core Web Vitals.

cards.q: State the limitation at the end of Node 13.
cards.a: Every technique so far assumes your code runs at a moment when the nodes it needs already exist, and nothing has said when that is.

cards.q: What is the most common beginner failure in the whole topic, and what kind of problem is it?
cards.a: document.querySelector('#thing') returning null. It is a timing problem, not a selector problem.

cards.q: What does a classic <script> tag do to the HTML parser?
cards.a: It blocks it. Parsing halts, the script is fetched if external and executed, and only then does parsing resume.

cards.q: Why does a script in <head> find every element null?
cards.a: Because parser blocking means it runs before the <body> has been parsed, so none of those nodes exist yet.

cards.q: Why is parser blocking the specified behaviour rather than an oversight?
cards.a: Because of document.write — a script was historically allowed to inject markup at its own position in the stream, so the parser could not safely run ahead.

cards.q: Name the three modern ways to make a script run after the tree exists.
cards.a: Place it at the end of <body>; use defer; or use type="module", which is deferred by default.

cards.q: What does <script defer> do?
cards.a: Downloads in parallel with parsing and executes after parsing completes. Multiple deferred scripts run in document order.

cards.q: What does <script async> do?
cards.a: Downloads in parallel and executes the moment it arrives — at an unpredictable time and in unpredictable order relative to other scripts.

cards.q: Which loading strategy suits a script that touches the DOM, and which suits analytics?
cards.a: defer (or a module) for anything touching the DOM; async only for genuinely independent scripts such as analytics.

cards.q: When does DOMContentLoaded fire?
cards.a: When the HTML has been fully parsed and all deferred scripts have run — the tree is complete. Stylesheets, images and subresources may still be loading.

cards.q: When does load fire?
cards.a: Later — when every subresource, including images, stylesheets and iframes, has finished.

cards.q: Why is waiting for load to initialise an interface a mistake?
cards.a: It is an unnecessary delay, sometimes of seconds, waiting for images that have nothing to do with whether your code can run.

cards.q: What are the three values of document.readyState?
cards.a: 'loading', 'interactive' (parsing done, equivalent to DOMContentLoaded), and 'complete' (equivalent to load).

cards.q: Why does checking readyState matter?
cards.a: A listener added for DOMContentLoaded after it has already fired will never run. Check readyState first and call your init directly if parsing is already done.

cards.q: Write the safe initialisation guard.
cards.a: if (document.readyState === 'loading') document.addEventListener('DOMContentLoaded', init); else init();

cards.q: What is the status of document.write?
cards.a: Effectively forbidden in new code. Called after parsing completes it wipes the entire document, and browsers block it for parser-inserted external scripts on slow connections.

cards.q: State the limitation at the end of Node 14.
cards.a: Everything attached, observed and created now stays attached forever, and in a page that navigates without reloading, that accumulates.

cards.q: When does JavaScript reclaim an object?
cards.a: When nothing can reach it any more. Reachability, not removal, is the criterion.

cards.q: What is a detached node?
cards.a: A DOM node removed from the document but still referenced by something, so it cannot be reclaimed. A growing set of them is the classic leaking-SPA memory profile.

cards.q: How does a listener on window leak a whole component?
cards.a: The handler closes over the component's nodes, and the listener is reachable from a global object, so the entire subtree stays alive after the component is gone.

cards.q: How does an observer leak?
cards.a: An observer that was never disconnect()ed keeps its targets alive, exactly as a global listener does.

cards.q: Why is an uncleared setInterval worse than a stray requestAnimationFrame?
cards.a: The interval keeps its callback — and everything it closes over — alive indefinitely, and keeps running in a hidden tab. requestAnimationFrame stops when the tab is hidden.

cards.q: Name the four reference chains that cause detached-node leaks.
cards.a: A global event listener; an un-disconnected observer; an uncleared timer or interval; and a cache — an array or map holding node references.

cards.q: Why is cleanup a correctness requirement rather than tidiness?
cards.a: Without it, a long-lived single-page application grows its memory footprint on every view change until it degrades or crashes. The document outlives every view rendered into it.

cards.q: What is the modern mechanism that makes listener teardown tractable?
cards.a: AbortController. Pass { signal: controller.signal } to every addEventListener, and one controller.abort() removes all of them.

cards.q: What does AbortController free you from having to keep?
cards.a: Named function references for every handler purely so removeEventListener can match them.

cards.q: Which framework concept is Node 15's teardown, exactly?
cards.a: A React useEffect cleanup function, or a framework's onDestroy/disconnectedCallback hook.

cards.q: How do you actually find these leaks?
cards.a: Chrome DevTools → Memory → Heap snapshot, with the Detached filter, comparing snapshots across repeated mount/unmount cycles.

cards.q: Does removing an element from the DOM free its memory?
cards.a: Only if nothing still references it. Removal is not deallocation.

cards.q: State the limitation at the end of Node 15.
cards.a: Even with perfect teardown, everything shares one namespace. Ids collide, any stylesheet can restyle anything, and a component cannot be dropped into an unknown page with confidence.

cards.t: Node 16 · Shadow DOM and custom elements
cards.q: What does el.attachShadow({ mode: 'open' }) return?
cards.a: A shadow root — the top of a second, separate tree attached to that element.

cards.t: Node 16 · Shadow DOM and custom elements
cards.q: How does a shadow tree relate to ordinary selectors from outside?
cards.a: It is invisible to them. document.querySelectorAll('.title') does not reach into a shadow tree.

cards.t: Node 16 · Shadow DOM and custom elements
cards.q: What happens to CSS at a shadow boundary?
cards.a: Styles defined inside do not leak out, and page styles do not leak in.

cards.t: Node 16 · Shadow DOM and custom elements
cards.q: Name the deliberate exceptions to shadow style encapsulation.
cards.a: Inherited properties such as color and font-family, and CSS custom properties, which pass through and are therefore the sanctioned theming mechanism.

cards.t: Node 16 · Shadow DOM and custom elements
cards.q: What does mode: 'closed' change, and is it a security boundary?
cards.a: It makes el.shadowRoot inaccessible from outside. It is not a security boundary and is rarely worth the cost.

cards.t: Node 16 · Shadow DOM and custom elements
cards.q: What is a <slot>?
cards.a: A placeholder inside a shadow tree marking where the host element's own children — its light DOM — should appear.

cards.t: Node 16 · Shadow DOM and custom elements
cards.q: Name the APIs that navigate between light and shadow trees.
cards.a: element.assignedSlot and slot.assignedNodes().

cards.t: Node 16 · Shadow DOM and custom elements
cards.q: How do you register a custom element?
cards.a: customElements.define('user-card', class extends HTMLElement { ... }). The tag name must contain a hyphen.

cards.t: Node 16 · Shadow DOM and custom elements
cards.q: Why must a custom element's tag name contain a hyphen?
cards.a: To guarantee it can never collide with a future standard HTML element name.

cards.t: Node 16 · Shadow DOM and custom elements
cards.q: Name the four custom element lifecycle callbacks.
cards.a: connectedCallback (inserted into the document), disconnectedCallback (removed), attributeChangedCallback (an observed attribute changed), adoptedCallback (moved between documents).

cards.t: Node 16 · Shadow DOM and custom elements
cards.q: Which callback is the natural home for Node 15's teardown?
cards.a: disconnectedCallback.

cards.t: Node 16 · Shadow DOM and custom elements
cards.q: How does a custom element declare which attributes it watches?
cards.a: A static observedAttributes getter returning an array of names. Only those trigger attributeChangedCallback.

cards.t: Node 16 · Shadow DOM and custom elements
cards.q: When did Custom Elements v1 and Shadow DOM v1 ship?
cards.a: Chrome 54 (2016), Safari 10.1 (2017), Firefox 63 (2018). The earlier v0 designs were abandoned.

cards.t: Node 16 · Shadow DOM and custom elements
cards.q: Give the honest assessment of Web Components' adoption.
cards.a: Genuinely right for a design system consumed by teams on different frameworks, and for widgets embedded in pages you do not control. Used far less than promised, because most teams already have a framework with a more ergonomic component model, and shadow boundaries complicate global styling, form participation and server rendering.

cards.t: Node 16 · Shadow DOM and custom elements
cards.q: What is event retargeting?
cards.a: An event crossing out of a shadow tree has its target rewritten to the host element rather than the internal node, preserving encapsulation.

cards.t: Node 16 · Shadow DOM and custom elements
cards.q: How do you see the full path an event took, including through shadow trees?
cards.a: e.composedPath().

cards.t: Node 16 · Shadow DOM and custom elements
cards.q: State the limitation at the end of Node 16.
cards.a: A <div> styled to look and behave like a button is still a <div> to a screen reader or keyboard user. Encapsulation guaranteed appearance and guaranteed nothing about usability.

cards.q: What is the accessibility tree?
cards.a: A parallel structure the browser derives from the DOM, exposing each node's role, name, value and state to assistive technology through the operating system.

cards.q: What does a screen reader actually read?
cards.a: The accessibility tree. It does not read your CSS.

cards.q: What does a native <button> provide for free?
cards.a: The button role, focusability, activation by both Enter and Space, and a name taken from its text content.

cards.q: What does a <div onclick> provide?
cards.a: None of that. It has a generic role, is not focusable, and cannot be activated from the keyboard.

cards.q: What is document.activeElement?
cards.a: The element that currently has focus.

cards.q: Which elements are focusable by default?
cards.a: Links with an href, form controls, buttons, and anything given a tabindex.

cards.q: What does tabindex="0" do?
cards.a: Puts the element into the natural tab order, at its document position.

cards.q: What does tabindex="-1" do, and when do you want it?
cards.a: Makes an element focusable programmatically but skipped by Tab. Used for a dialog container you want to move focus into.

cards.q: Why are positive tabindex values almost always a mistake?
cards.a: They override document order globally and produce a tab sequence nobody can predict or maintain.

cards.q: How are ARIA attributes set from JavaScript?
cards.a: As ordinary DOM attributes — el.setAttribute('aria-expanded', 'true'). Keeping them synchronised with visual state is normal DOM work, not a separate discipline.

cards.q: Name commonly used ARIA attributes.
cards.a: role, aria-expanded, aria-selected, aria-label, aria-labelledby, aria-describedby, aria-live, aria-hidden, aria-current.

cards.q: State the most-quoted rule of ARIA and why it is true.
cards.a: No ARIA is better than bad ARIA. An incorrect role actively misleads a screen reader user, where a plain <div> merely says nothing.

cards.q: State the first rule of ARIA.
cards.a: Do not use it — use the native element that already has the semantics you want.

cards.q: What must happen to focus when a modal dialog opens and closes?
cards.a: It must move into the dialog on open, be trapped inside while open, and return to the trigger on close.

cards.q: What does the inert attribute do, and when did it ship?
cards.a: Makes an entire subtree unfocusable and invisible to assistive technology. Chrome 102 (2022), Safari 15.5, Firefox 112 (2023).

cards.q: Why is <dialog> with showModal() the correct default?
cards.a: It handles focus movement, inerting the rest of the page, the top layer, and the Escape key natively.

cards.q: What does aria-live solve?
cards.a: Announcing content that changes without user action — a toast, a validation summary, a live result count — which a screen reader would otherwise never mention.

cards.q: State the limitation at the end of Node 17.
cards.a: All of this assumed the markup came from you. The moment a string arrives from a user, an API or a CMS and becomes nodes, every guarantee is only as good as that string.

cards.q: Define cross-site scripting.
cards.a: The vulnerability class where attacker-controlled text becomes executing code inside another user's page, in your origin.

cards.q: What makes the DOM-based variant of XSS distinctive?
cards.a: It needs no server involvement at all. A value read from location.hash or a query parameter and passed to innerHTML is enough.

cards.q: What can injected code do once it runs in your origin?
cards.a: Read cookies not marked HttpOnly, read localStorage, issue authenticated requests as the user, and rewrite the page.

cards.q: List the XSS defences in the order you should reach for them.
cards.a: 1) textContent for anything that is text. 2) Build nodes with createElement and set properties. 3) If HTML must be accepted, sanitise with a maintained library such as DOMPurify.

cards.q: Why must you never sanitise HTML with a regular expression?
cards.a: The space of encodings, nesting and parser quirks is far larger than it looks, and the HTML parser's repair behaviour can turn a string your regex approved into markup it did not anticipate.

cards.q: How does a Content Security Policy help?
cards.a: It restricts what a page may execute. A policy without 'unsafe-inline' neutralises whole categories of injection even when a bug exists.

cards.q: What do Trusted Types do, and what is their availability?
cards.a: They make assigning a plain string to innerHTML throw, so dangerous sinks accept only values that passed through a policy function you wrote. Chrome 83 (2020), still Chromium-only.

cards.q: What does new DOMParser().parseFromString(str, 'text/html') produce?
cards.a: A complete, inert Document — nothing renders, no scripts run, no images are fetched — which you can query with everything from Nodes 2 and 3 before deciding what to adopt.

cards.q: How do you move a node from a parsed document into the live one?
cards.a: document.importNode(node, true) for a copy, or document.adoptNode(node) to move it.

cards.q: What does XMLSerializer or outerHTML give you?
cards.a: A string serialisation of the nodes — but of the repaired tree, not the markup you originally wrote.

cards.q: Why does innerHTML parsing depend on the element you assign it to?
cards.a: The HTML parser has context-sensitive rules. A <tr> string assigned to a <div> has its tags discarded, because rows are only valid inside table sections.

cards.q: State the limitation at the end of Node 18.
cards.a: Nothing in this chain is wrong, and doing all of it by hand at application scale means manually keeping a tree of nodes in agreement with a set of application state, forever.

cards.t: Node 19 · What frameworks took, and what they did not
cards.q: What question does every DOM operation answer, and what question does an application want answered?
cards.a: Every DOM operation answers how do I change this. An application wants to answer given this state, what should be on screen.

cards.t: Node 19 · What frameworks took, and what they did not
cards.q: Why does hand-writing that bridge scale badly?
cards.a: For every state change you must write the specific sequence of mutations transforming the current DOM into the correct one, and the number of transitions grows far faster than the number of states.

cards.t: Node 19 · What frameworks took, and what they did not
cards.q: When was React released?
cards.a: May 2013.

cards.t: Node 19 · What frameworks took, and what they did not
cards.q: State the trade React makes.
cards.a: You write a function from state to a description of the desired tree, and the framework computes and applies the mutations.

cards.t: Node 19 · What frameworks took, and what they did not
cards.q: What is a virtual DOM, precisely?
cards.a: A plain-object description of the desired tree, cheap to build and discard, diffed against the previous description to derive a minimal set of real DOM operations.

cards.t: Node 19 · What frameworks took, and what they did not
cards.q: How do Svelte and Solid reach the same goal differently?
cards.a: Svelte compiles the mutations at build time. Solid and Vue's reactivity track dependencies at the value level and update precisely the nodes affected. The trade is identical: you write a description, not mutations.

cards.t: Node 19 · What frameworks took, and what they did not
cards.q: Which node of the chain does a framework actually replace?
cards.a: Node 6 — the manual construction and mutation of nodes. Every other node remains in force.

cards.t: Node 19 · What frameworks took, and what they did not
cards.q: What is React's synthetic event system, in terms of this chain?
cards.a: A delegation layer — Nodes 7 through 9 unchanged. Handlers receive an object with the same target, currentTarget, stopPropagation and preventDefault.

cards.t: Node 19 · What frameworks took, and what they did not
cards.q: Why does React use className rather than class?
cards.a: It sets the DOM property, and the property name is className because class is a reserved word in JavaScript. This is the Node 5 attribute/property split surfacing in the API.

cards.t: Node 19 · What frameworks took, and what they did not
cards.q: Which node explains React's controlled inputs?
cards.a: Node 5 — the value attribute is the initial value while input.value is live state, so React must drive the property to own the value.

cards.t: Node 19 · What frameworks took, and what they did not
cards.q: What is useEffect's cleanup function, in terms of this chain?
cards.a: Node 15's teardown, unchanged — remove listeners, disconnect observers, clear timers.

cards.t: Node 19 · What frameworks took, and what they did not
cards.q: Why does useRef exist?
cards.a: Because measurement (Node 11), focus management (Node 17), and third-party integration all need a real node, which a description of a tree does not give you.

cards.t: Node 19 · What frameworks took, and what they did not
cards.q: Does React prevent layout thrashing?
cards.a: No. Node 12 applies unchanged — reading geometry in a component still forces layout exactly as it does in plain DOM code.

cards.t: Node 19 · What frameworks took, and what they did not
cards.q: What is the key prop asking for, in DOM terms?
cards.a: Identity information the diffing algorithm needs, made necessary by Node 6's rule that a node has one parent and insertion moves rather than copies.

cards.t: Node 19 · What frameworks took, and what they did not
cards.q: Why are “I know React” and “I know the DOM” different claims?
cards.a: React replaces node construction only. Events, propagation, geometry, focus, accessibility, layout cost and teardown are all still yours — and they are what you will be debugging.

cards.t: Node 19 · What frameworks took, and what they did not
cards.q: Sum up the chain's closing argument in one sentence.
cards.a: Frameworks replaced the node-building layer and left every other link in the chain exactly where it was, which is why the DOM is what makes a framework debuggable.
